title: The Call of Duty and the Predicament of the Hero
paragraphs: There might be many reasons for men to leave women. Separation means unbearable anxiety for women. The man takes much pains to console his woman and take leave of her. Separation is inevitable for men. They must go to train in warfare or to acquire knowledge for enriching their minds. If trained in these skills, separation happens on account of protection of the state leaving behind the object of one’s love.

The woman doesn’t take the parting for good, though her loneliness is rather short. Since both of them live so intimately as not to let a thread to pass through their embrace, she regards each day of separation as a sword chopping her heart.

Even though he parts only to learn Tamiḻ literature and grammar and receive training in warfare after explaining the benefits of his activities to the home and the country, she bids adieu only after shedding copious tears, waterfall like.

If the hero happens to be a king bound by the responsibilities of the state such as aiding a friendly ruler, or if he goes on an ambassadorial mission, he has to be valorous or wise as the occasion demands.

He measures his own strength, his army’s strength, and ally’s strength, while the superiority of his foe in foot-soldiers,cavalry, and elephant force also does not escape his thoughts. In spite of all these reflections flashing across his mind, and in spite of his resolution to encounter the odds and triumph over them, he marches ahead only after seeking farewell from his darling. Since it involves the responsibility of protecting the country, the lady bids farewell wishing him victory, though her eyes shed tears like the Ganga and the Cauvery.
In the warfield, caught like a tiger in the midst of elephants, he comes unscathed due to strength of determination.

The war still persists, and the hero demonstrates that he is second to none. Then, at night, in the war-camp, his fair lady disturbs him in the dream. Since even the act of pining for her in dreams would dampen his heroic vigour, he avoids it.

The war ends, with the hoisting of the flag of victory. He hastens the chariot driver. “The sweet lady of mine would be waiting; her passionate kisses would heal my injuries. Go fast”, he says. “Horses, may God bless you to run like a storm and convey me to my wife”, he requests from the core of his heart.
On the way, occasionally, on encountering a prostitute he makes merry. Since this news would reach the ears of his love waiting at home, it would lead to sulking.
He should resolve that sulking also and row the boat of marital life in the river of happiness. The poetic hero has many such responsibilities and duties, and predicaments as well:

> As he intends going after mind’s enrichment and physical prowess > And the rewards attendant therein; > As he dilates to the heroine > Upon the abiding note such quests yield, > And upon the ignominy keeping off these quests would result in; > As he responds to the calling of being a royal emissary; > As he takes to aiding an ally in need; > As he sets out to take on hostile foemen > Who pride over their might, the might of their allies and the difficulty of > invading their forts > And over the secured unapproachability of their fortresses; > And as he remains in a war-camp away from his love; > As he, > Returning after the task accomplished,

> Addresses his charioteer urging him to make it swift; > As he parts from his love > For purpose of security and protection of the state; > And, > As he importunes her > After his return from prostitutes > And seeks resolution of her sulking. > (Poruḷatikāram : Akattiṇai iyal, verse 41)
